extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students and instructors in algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Construction and properties of CW approximations, n-connected CW models, Postnikov towers, and related homotopy-theoretic tools (cellular approximation, excision ranges, suspension theorems). Includes stepwise procedures for attaching cells to achieve desired effects on homotopy groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 4.10: local PL replacement when attaching a cell
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f: I^n → Z where Z is obtained from a subspace W by attaching a cell e^k, there is a homotopy f_t from f = f_0 to f_1 for which there is a polyhedron K ⊂ I^n such that (a) f_1(K) ⊂ e^k and f_1|K is PL with respect to some identification of e^k with R^k, and (b) K ⊃ f_1^{-1}(U) for some nonempty open set U in e^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deform maps into a cell so that on a polyhedral subset the map is piecewise-linear and contains the preimage of some open set in the cell. Proof strategy: choose concentric balls in the cell, use uniform continuity to subdivide I^n into small cubes, form K as unions of cubes meeting preimages, subdivide into simplices, define g linear on simplices agreeing with f on vertices, build homotopy (1 - tφ)f + tφ g where φ is a simplexwise linear cutoff. Consequence: if n < k one can arrange the homotoped map to miss points in the k-cell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular approximation for pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Every map f:(X,A)→(Y,B) of CW pairs can be deformed through maps of pairs to a cellular map; the homotopy may be taken stationary on any subcomplex of X where f is already cellular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cellular approximation inductively: first deform restriction f|A to be cellular, extend to X, then deform on cells of X one dimension at a time while fixing A. The deformation can be performed rel any subcomplex where f is already cellular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: weak homotopy equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f:X→Y is a weak homotopy equivalence if it induces isomorphisms π_n(X,x_0) → π_n(Y,f(x_0)) for all n ≥ 0 and all choices of basepoint x_0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitehead's theorem: between CW complexes (or spaces homotopy equivalent to CW complexes) a weak homotopy equivalence is a homotopy equivalence. Weak homotopy equivalence preserves homology and cohomology (Proposition 4.21) and induces bijections on homotopy classes of maps from CW complexes (Proposition 4.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of CW approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: For every space X there exists a CW complex Z and a weak homotopy equivalence f: Z → X (a CW approximation). If X is path-connected, Z may be chosen with a single 0-cell and all higher cells attached by basepoint-preserving maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct inductively by starting with a 0-cell for each path component, then attach 1-cells to make π_1 surjective, attach 2-cells to make π_1 an isomorphism and π_2 surjective, and continue. At each stage attach cells to address kernels and generators of homotopy groups so that after attaching k-cells the map is injective on π_{k-1} and surjective on π_k (see the property (*) described in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attaching k-cells to enforce injectivity/surjectivity on π_i
rubrics_metrics.description: Given A with map f:A→X and k≥0, attach k-cells to A in two steps so that the extended map f:B→X satisfies: for each chosen basepoint a_γ the induced f_*: π_i(B,a_γ) → π_i(X,f(a_γ)) is injective for i = k−1 (when k>0) and surjective for i = k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step (1) (when k>0): choose cellular maps φ_α:(S^{k−1},s_0)→(A,a_γ) representing generators of kernels of f_*:π_{k−1}(A,a_γ)→π_{k−1}(X,f(a_γ)), attach k-cells along these maps and extend f via nullhomotopies. Step (2): choose maps f_β:S^k → X representing generators of π_k(X,f(a_γ)), attach k-cells to A via constant maps at basepoints and extend f over the resulting S^k via f_β. Remarks: it suffices to attach cells for generators (not all elements); attaching k-cells does not affect π_i for i < k−1.

rubrics_metrics.name: n-connected CW model (definition and existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An n-connected CW model for a pair (X,A) (with A a nonempty CW complex) is an n-connected CW pair (Z,A) and a map f:Z→X with f|A = id such that f_*: π_i(Z)→π_i(X) is an isomorphism for i > n and an injection for i = n, for all basepoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such models exist for all n≥0 and can be chosen so that Z is obtained from A by attaching cells of dimension > n (Proposition 4.17). The construction proceeds by attaching cells to A to kill unwanted relative homotopy and to create required surjectivity, analogous to the CW-approximation construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and functoriality of n-connected models (Proposition 4.18 & Corollary 4.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n-connected model f:(Z,A)→(X,A) and n'–connected model f':(Z',A')→(X',A') and a map g:(X,A)→(X',A'), if n ≥ n' there exists h:Z→Z' with h|A = g and gf ≃ f' h rel A; such h is unique up to homotopy rel A. Consequently, n-connected CW models are unique up to homotopy equivalence rel A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mapping cylinders and the compression lemma; one may assume cells of Z−A have dimension > n to apply dimension-connectivity arguments. This yields functorial maps between models and allows building towers of models for varying n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postnikov truncation properties (Example 4.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each connected CW complex X and integer n ≥ 1 there exists a CW complex X_n containing X as a subcomplex such that (a) π_i(X_n) = 0 for i > n, and (b) the inclusion X → X_n induces an isomorphism on π_i for i ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by attaching cells of dimension ≥ n+2 to kill higher homotopy groups successively. The inclusions X → X_n are compatible to form a Postnikov tower; X_{n+1} maps to X_n and extension lemmas apply because of vanishing higher π_i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak homotopy equivalence preserves homology and cohomology (Proposition 4.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak homotopy equivalence f:X→Y induces isomorphisms f_*: H_n(X;G) → H_n(Y;G) and f^*: H^n(Y;G) → H^n(X;G) for all n and all coefficient groups G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via mapping cylinder Mf: show that if (Z,X) is an n-connected pair then H_i(Z,X;G)=0 and H^i(Z,X;G)=0 for i ≤ n; use finite simplicial approximation of singular cycles and the compression lemma to homotope maps into X when relative π_i vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak homotopy equivalences induce bijections on homotopy classes (Proposition 4.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:Y → Z is a weak homotopy equivalence then for every CW complex X the induced maps [X,Y] → [X,Z] and ⟨X,Y⟩ → ⟨X,Z⟩ (pointed homotopy classes) are bijections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace f by an inclusion via its mapping cylinder Mf; relative homotopy groups π_n(Z,Y,y_0) vanish, so by the compression lemma any map X→Z can be homotoped to lie in Y, giving surjectivity; a relative version gives injectivity. For pointed maps use the reduced mapping cylinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression lemma (practical criterion used throughout)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π_i(W,Z)=0 for i ≤ k (relative groups vanish up to a dimension), then any map (K,L)→(W,Z) from a CW pair with dim K ≤ k can be homotoped rel L to have image in Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to deform maps or homotopies into subcomplexes when relative homotopy groups vanish up to a suitable dimension; central in proofs of existence/uniqueness of CW models, excision for homotopy groups, and bijectivity results for [X,−].

rubrics_metrics.name: Excision range for homotopy groups (Theorem 4.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X = A ∪ B with C = A ∩ B nonempty and connected. If (A,C) is m-connected and (B,C) is n-connected (m,n ≥ 0), then the inclusion π_i(A,C) → π_i(X,B) is an isomorphism for i < m + n and a surjection for i = m + n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by handling successively more general attaching-cell cases, using Lemma 4.10 to arrange maps so preimages are polyhedral and then constructing separating functions to excise undesired parts of the domain. The theorem yields the Freudenthal suspension range and underlies many suspension/excision arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freudenthal suspension theorem (Corollary 4.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspension map π_i(S^n) → π_{i+1}(S^{n+1}) is an isomorphism for i < 2n−1 and a surjection for i = 2n−1. More generally, for X an (n−1)-connected CW complex the suspension π_i(X) → π_{i+1}(SX) satisfies the same range statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduce by decomposing the suspension SX as union of two cones intersecting in X and applying Theorem 4.23 to the pair of cones. This is the key input for computing stable homotopy in low ranges and for proving π_n(S^n) ≅ Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree/classification of π_n(S^n) (Corollary 4.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: For all n ≥ 1, π_n(S^n) ≅ Z, generated by the identity map; the degree map π_n(S^n) → Z is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: suspension maps give isomorphisms from π_1(S^1) ≅ Z up to π_n(S^n); degree can be shown infinite via either homology (existence of maps of arbitrary degree) or via the Hopf fibration giving π_1(S^1) ≅ π_2(S^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attaching k-cells does not affect low-dimensional homotopy
rubrics_metrics.description: Attaching k-cells to a CW complex does not affect π_i for i < k−1; in particular, attaching higher-dimensional cells preserves previously established isomorphisms or surjectivities in lower dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used repeatedly in inductive constructions (CW approximations, n-connected models) to argue that earlier properties remain valid after further attachments. It follows from cellular approximation and homotopy-theoretic dimension bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: CW-approximation and product compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are CW approximations to spaces Z and W respectively, then X × Y (with the CW topology) is a CW approximation to Z × W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CW product has the same compact sets as the product topology, so homotopy groups are preserved; this allows extension of results (e.g., Künneth formula) from CW complexes to arbitrary spaces by passing to CW approximations.
